figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Autonomous whole-body behavior in real-world environments the robot has never seen. In each environment, the robot is acting in response to a natural-language instruction. The robot sees only its own egocentric camera feed. No scene is scanned and no trajectory is scripted.
figures.headline: Real-world runs show the robot acting on language instructions in homes it has never seen, using only its own camera feed.
citing_sentences: Some of the real-world environments are shown in Fig. 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Onboard autonomy stack. (A) A VLM ($\sim$0.5 Hz) processes a natural-language request and egocentric visual input (top left) and outputs a sequence of subtasks. (B) The motion generator ($\sim$3 Hz) maps each subtask and the corresponding egocentric RGB frames into a $5\,$s whole-body motion plan. (C) The motion tracker ($50\,$Hz) executes the motion plan, grounding the trajectory into the physical world using egocentric depth (bottom left) and proprioception.
figures.headline: The stack has three layers running at about 0.5 Hz, 3 Hz and 50 Hz, from language subtasks down to joint commands.
citing_sentences: The HALO autonomy stack has three layers, illustrated in Fig. 2.
The onboard autonomy stack has three layers, shown in Fig. 2.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Synthetic data generation and training pipeline. (A) Each task is decomposed into segments defined by text prompts and keyframe poses. After sampling target asset locations and routing navigation waypoints, a conditional diffusion model synthesizes motion segments from these constraints, stitching them into a continuous whole-body trajectory. (B) This generated trajectory and its associated assets are embedded into procedurally generated scenes, ensuring collision-free placement. (C) A simulator replays the kinematic motion to render egocentric vision from the robot’s head-mounted cameras. Visual domain randomization is applied to maximize appearance diversity. (D) The resulting corpus is used for training the autonomy stack, via imitation learning for the motion generator and via reinforcement learning for the motion tracker.
figures.headline: The synthetic pipeline chains motion segments into trajectories, places them in generated rooms, and renders egocentric video for training.
citing_sentences: The synthetic data generation pipeline is shown in Fig. 3 and detailed in Section -A.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Procedural rooms and scene baking. Top: path-traced training rooms from Infinigen. Bottom: a held-out view of a dense living room rendered from the bake in three engines, where the mean absolute error relative to path tracing is $4.2$ (Blender), $4.5$ (MuJoCo) and $4.7$ (Isaac Sim) grey levels and mostly lies in the light pool of the lamp on the floor and at object edges (error map: white is $0$, dark blue is $32$ grey levels or more).
figures.headline: Baked renders of a dense living room differ from path tracing by 4.2 to 4.7 grey levels across three renderers.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Episodes of the six skills. Top: training frames from the egocentric fisheye camera ($1280\mathbin{\!\times\!}800$). Bottom: a typical episode of each skill on the same time axis (blue triangles are full-body keyframes), where only Sit chains several Kimodo calls.
figures.headline: A typical episode of each of the six skills is shown, with only the Sit skill chaining several motion generation calls.
citing_sentences: We use Kimodo [9] to generate the motions, with a classifier-free guidance weight of $2.0$ on both the text and the constraints (root paths and full-body keyframes in Fig. 5).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Motion tracker onboard inference architecture. On the Jetson Orin NX, the tracker runs at $50\,$Hz and fuses three onboard streams: (top left) raw stereo IR frames from the RealSense D435i (emitter off) are mapped by LiteAnyStereo [45] (TensorRT FP16) to a clean $48\mathbin{\!\times\!}84$ egocentric depth image and encoded by a 2D CNN; (bottom left) a $30$-step proprioceptive history together with the next $30$ plan frames is encoded by a 1D temporal CNN; and (center) both feature vectors are concatenated with the current proprioceptive state and $5$-frame motion plan lookahead and passed through a SimBa residual MLP [49] to output $29$ target joint positions for the low-level PD controller.
figures.headline: The tracker fuses a 48×84 depth image, a 30-step proprioceptive history and the motion plan to output 29 joint targets at 50 Hz.
citing_sentences: 6) drops all world-frame velocities and link poses, observing only noisy IMU angular velocity and gravity, joint positions and velocities, the previous action, the pelvis orientation error, a shorter $5$-frame ($0.1\,$s) reference window, the next 30 plan frames, a $30$-step history, and a $48\mathbin{\!\times\!}84$ depth image.

As shown in Fig. 6 and Table VI, a 3-layer 1D CNN encodes the $30$-step observation history, and a 4-layer stride-$2$ 2D CNN encodes the $48\mathbin{\!\times\!}84$ depth image (or a 3-layer 2D CNN over the $17\mathbin{\!\times\!}11$ height map for the experts and critics).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Communication graph. The generator pulls the robot state (get_state) and the not-yet-executed reference (get_trim) from the tracker and sends each new motion plan (put_plan). The orchestrator sends the current subtask to the generator (subtask) and receives the egocentric frame (obs) and the generator’s motion status (gen_status). The web GUI subscribes to state, obs, subtask, and plan.
figures.headline: The communication graph shows the generator exchanging plans with the tracker, and the orchestrator exchanging subtasks and frames with the generator.
citing_sentences: Fig. 7 shows the processes and channels.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Onboard compute and sensing. A Mac mini M4 Pro in the rear enclosure runs the orchestrator (∼0.5 Hz) and the motion generator (∼3 Hz). The robot’s Jetson Orin NX runs the motion tracker in a $50\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ real-time loop. The OAK-1W supplies the $120^{\circ}$ RGB the generator reasons over; the RealSense D435i supplies the $55^{\circ}$ depth the tracker reacts to. All modules run onboard, with external network calls used only when querying an optional cloud VLM for orchestration.
figures.headline: Orchestration and generation run on a Mac mini, while the 50 Hz tracker runs on the robot's onboard Jetson module.

abstract: Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale. Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data. We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor. HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-halo/ for code and videos.

sections.body: Humanoid control needs paired egocentric images, instructions, and whole-body joint trajectories, and no corpus of this data exists at scale. Teleoperation and wearable capture cost at least an hour of human time per hour of data. HALO generates the data in simulation: a motion diffusion model produces whole-body motion, a procedural generator supplies rooms, and a simulator renders the egocentric video. The training corpus comprises 300 hours of episodes across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The onboard stack has an orchestrator invoked every two seconds, a motion generator at 3 Hz that outputs five seconds of joint angles and pelvis poses, and a 50 Hz motion tracker that uses onboard depth and proprioception.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Humanoid robots need paired vision-language-motion data, which HALO generates in simulation instead of by teleoperation.

sections.body: Prior systems use recorded human motion, reconstruct or hand-author environments, or pass generated motion to trackers that cannot see. HALO generates trajectories with a kinematic motion diffusion model trained on human motion, then discards invalid ones with geometric verification. VLK trains inside two pre-scanned rooms, GRAIL restricts object interaction to authored templates, and FetchMan generates a large set of scenes for one reach-and-pick task. HALO trains across a thousand procedurally generated homes. Table I reports 360 real trials over 6 environments for HALO, against 120 over 2 for VLK and 45 over 3 for TANGO. Table I marks GRAIL's perceptive tracker as partial and HALO's as present.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work relies on scanned rooms, authored templates, or blind trackers; HALO pairs procedural homes with a perceptive tracker.

sections.body: The stack has three layers. The motion generator maps an egocentric RGB image and a subtask to a 5-second, 30 Hz plan of 29 joint angles and a relative pelvis pose, 36 values per frame. It uses a frozen Qwen3.5-2B encoder, an eight-block diffusion transformer of width 512 trained by flow matching, and 15 Euler steps at inference. Asynchronous generation passes the first 15 committed frames as clean tokens so the model learns continuity with the plan it follows. The tracker is trained in three phases: privileged PPO experts for each skill, distillation into one depth-based student, and multi-critic PPO fine-tuning of the student with depth in the loop.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: A frozen vision-language encoder and a flow-matching decoder generate 5-second motion plans that a depth-conditioned tracker executes.

sections.body: Training uses 300 hours of episodes over 1,000 homes, generated in 48 hours on 250 H100 GPUs. Table II reports single-task success of 91% in simulation and 91% in real trials, with Go-To at 98 and 92, Sit at 84 and 85, and Crawl at 84 and 90. Chained tasks score lower: Door→Go-To reaches 71 in simulation and 100 in the real world, Crouch→Sit 73 and 60, and Crouch→Go-To→Push 64 and 50. The authors attribute chain failures to the next subtask starting with its target out of view. For example, 3 of 5 failed real trials ended a crouch with the head turned away from the box. The authors suggest adding search and turn-in-place recovery behaviors.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Single-task success averages 91% in simulation and reality, while chained multi-task success falls to 69% and 70%.

sections.body: The authors conclude that simulation can serve as the data engine for humanoid autonomy, with the stack transferring zero-shot to real environments. They list four limitations. Adding a task still requires a person to write its prompt and author its keyframes. Vision gives no direct perception of contact, so an object that leaves the camera's view leaves the policy with no signal, and contact-rich tasks degrade. The interface between generator and tracker is narrow, because the tracker does not know what its plan is for. The orchestration layer is relatively simple, and a larger repertoire of tasks would likely need a more agentic system.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Simulation can supply humanoid training data, but task authoring, contact sensing, the generator-tracker interface and orchestration remain limits.

sections.body: The appendix covers the corpus and its generation. Six skill datasets total 296.3 hours at 30 Hz. Infinigen generated 1,200 rooms; 1,000 are used for training and 178 are held out. Baking lighting avoids slow path tracing, and the median bake error is 2.0 on the eight projected views and 3.8 on 16 held-out views. Kimodo produces the motions, and candidate trajectories are scored by checks such as 33 for Sit. Rendering randomizes exposure, noise, and dome light. The discussion reports that a fine-tuned encoder recognized only the one human model in training, and that a black frame on 30% of samples forced the model to follow the command.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix details the six-skill corpus, scene generation, baking error, motion filtering, rendering and generator and tracker design.
